stories.topic: How Seeing Like a State Sat on the Shelf for Eight Years
stories.summary: When Lant Pritchett moved to Delhi after the UPA came to power in 2004, he handed Ajay two books — Seeing Like a State and Chester Barnard's The Functions of the Executive — saying they would change how he thought about the world. Ajay didn't read it until 2012. When he finally did, every page felt like an assault on what he had believed; he blew off all his meetings and just sat reading for two days, breathlessly arguing back with the book.
stories.insight: A small testament to the physicality of unread books — the shelf is part of the apparatus of the mind, and the right book waits for the right reader. Ajay's permission slip to the listener: don't beat yourself up about the unread shelf. The day will come when you pull a book out, and that delay was part of the encounter.

stories.topic: Why Newton Was a Mean Man Who Stood on Hooke
stories.summary: Riffing on the 'shoulders of giants' line, Ajay points out the original quote is Newton's — and Newton was a 'truly mean and unpleasant person' locked in lifelong rivalry with Robert Hooke. Hooke was a hunchback. Newton's 'shoulders of giants' line was, in part, a cruel jibe — implying Hooke wasn't tall enough to be one.
stories.insight: A reminder that great minds and good people are orthogonal axes — neither negatively correlated nor positively. The history of ideas is messier than the canonical quotations suggest, and the rivalries behind the lines are often petty and human.

stories.topic: Stalin's Ukraine and the Long Memory of Collectivisation
stories.summary: Stalin, despite being capable of pragmatism, was a 'bloodyminded ideologue' on collectivisation. When rich Ukrainian farmers resisted, he crushed them with extraordinary brutality, blocking food into Ukraine and seizing all its grain. Between 4% and 10% of the population died in a man-made famine — the Holodomor. In 1991, 90% of Ukraine voted to leave Russia. The seeds of that vote were sown in 1932.
stories.insight: A grand state legibility scheme can be paid for many decades later — the ledger of state coercion runs on a generational timescale. Today's Russia-Ukraine antagonism is, in part, the long shadow of one high-modernist scheme.

stories.topic: Why the USSR's Crude-for-Grain Economy Collapsed
stories.summary: By the mid-80s the Soviet economy ran on a tense balance: export crude oil, import grain. When the world price of crude went down and the price of grain went up, the model snapped. The country couldn't feed itself because Stalin's collectivisation had broken Soviet agriculture half a century earlier.
stories.insight: There is a direct line from the 1932 collectivisation to the 1991 collapse — the high-modernist scheme to remake agriculture not only killed millions but locked the USSR into a fragile commodity dependency that made eventual collapse a matter of price movements.

stories.topic: Aadhaar Was Built Without Its Privacy Law
stories.summary: The first Aadhaar number was issued in 2009. Ajay was in those debates. The deal was: build the unique-ID system now, the privacy law will follow. Manmohan Singh's government was supposed to deliver it. James C Scott was 'slapping me around' from 2012 onwards. Older and wiser, Ajay now thinks the train should never have left the station without a powerful privacy law in place first.
stories.insight: State legibility schemes have a one-way ratchet. Once the data infrastructure is built, you can't un-build it — and the promised checks and balances tend to never arrive. The order of operations matters: privacy law first, surveillance system second.

stories.summary: Amit was born in Chandigarh, designed by Le Corbusier — one of the great villains of high modernism. Walking around it with friends recently, he could feel the seductive surface — wide roads, clean air, looks nice. But underneath he knew the unseen cost: the sterile geometry, the absence of the organic life that makes a city actually alive.
stories.insight: The seen of high-modernism is always real — wider roads, cleaner air, neat geometry. The cost is everything you can't see — the spontaneous order that makes a city live. Bombay is not Chandigarh; the great living city is not the planned one.

stories.topic: The 100,000 Words on Jane Jacobs Cut From The Power Broker
stories.summary: The Power Broker by Robert Caro was originally over a million words; the publisher said the paper grammage couldn't take it. So an entire 100,000-word section on Jane Jacobs was cut to keep the binding from falling apart. The two opposing philosophies of high-modernism (Robert Moses) and metis (Jane Jacobs) almost lived inside one book.
stories.insight: The physical constraints of the book object once shaped the intellectual canon as much as ideas did. We will never read the missing chapter on Jacobs — the shape of even our greatest non-fiction is partly a function of glue, paper, and binding.

stories.summary: At eighteen or nineteen, Amit and his friend Rupesh tried to stage Girish Karnad's Tughlaq as a two-man play. Inevitably, one of them was Bengali and the Hindi requirement clashed; the project collapsed into procrastination and never happened.
stories.insight: A self-deprecating teaser that doubles as a cultural pointer: Karnad wrote Tughlaq in the mid-60s as a vehicle for the disillusionment with Nehruvian socialism — a play about the high-modernist Tughlaq was, in disguise, a play about Nehru. Great men contain multitudes, and great follies can be made by great men.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: The book the entire episode is built around — Scott's 1998 study of why grand top-down schemes by states tend to fail.
recommendations.reason: A book of multiple mind-blowing ideas — state legibility, high modernism, metis, the four-part test for catastrophe — each of which is an engine for thinking about the world. The book that broadens after Scott's earlier narrower work, written by a thinker who by 1998 was working as a renaissance mind across political philosophy, sociology, anthropology, urban policy, and development studies.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier episode on the theory of change.
recommendations.reason: The right frame for why James C Scott matters even when no single reader makes him famous. You don't have to shoot for B2C success in everything you do — the path to a better world runs through ideas that reshape culture, with many runners passing the baton. Scott is one of those baton-runners.

recommendations.item: Forests, Trees, and Intellectual Roots... (review of Seeing Like a State)
recommendations.creator: Brad DeLong
recommendations.context: DeLong's blog review of Seeing Like a State that originally flagged the book.
recommendations.reason: Ajay missed the book in 1998 and missed DeLong's 1990s blog flag in his RSS feed; the review is still worth reading as one of the most substantive engagements with Scott's argument by an economist.

recommendations.creator: Chester Barnard
recommendations.context: The other book Lant Pritchett handed Ajay in 2004 alongside Seeing Like a State.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett bracketed the two as the books that would change how Ajay thought about the world — Barnard on how organisations actually work from the inside, Scott on how states actually see from the outside. Recommended in the same breath.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode that touched on Nehru and Indian leadership.
recommendations.reason: Where Ajay laid out his love for Nehru as a 'great artist' even while believing his economic art was bad — the model for how to separate the man from the policy in evaluating high-modernist leaders.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier episode on the four metrics of complexity for state interventions.
recommendations.reason: Maps directly onto the problem of state legibility — discretion, number of transactions, stakes, and opacity are all the conditions under which a bureaucracy struggles to see correctly. The framework is the operational underbelly of Scott's seeing-like-a-state argument.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Ep 56 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the endless amassing and perpetual storage of data by the state.
recommendations.reason: Where Ajay argued that data deletion should be the default — the state's baseline should be to delete acquired data within seconds, with non-deletion needing to be authorised by the people exactly as state coercion already is. A constitutional principle that flows directly from Scott's warning about state legibility.

recommendations.item: A Passion for Cycling (Ep 53 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's cycling episode, suggested as a starting point for the listener challenge to map any EIE episode onto Seeing Like a State.
recommendations.reason: A formation of cyclists in slipstream looks like high-modernist control; but a true fan also knows the 'washing-machine effect' near a sprint finish, which is spontaneous order in chaos. The episode contains both of Scott's polarities lurking in plain sight.

recommendations.creator: Freedom House
recommendations.context: Freedom House's annual ranking of democracies, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bottom.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's proposed unit of analysis for stage two of Scott's project — the appropriate state legibility mechanism should vary with the country's place on the Freedom House list. The next hundred years of research is to derive the thumb rules: what is safe in Norway is a prison in North Korea.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on subsidiarity in Indian governance.
recommendations.reason: The constitutional implication of Scott's argument for India: a 3.3-million-square-kilometre country with a thousand locales cannot be governed by one dictator. Push every function down to the lowest level of government at which it can be done — let a thousand flowers bloom.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Ep 37 of EIE)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode applying high-modernism vs metis to firms.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's example of how Scott's toolkit travels — once you take it into your brain, you start seeing imperial firms (one process, one manual, one nation) versus adaptive firms (UP is not Maharashtra). Different strokes for different situations, applied inside the corporation.

recommendations.creator: Robert Caro
recommendations.context: Caro's biography of Robert Moses, master planner of New York City.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece that is at once a biography of a man, of a city, and a study of how power can be used and misused. Robert Moses did the high-modernism of New York — top-down design of bridges, parks, expressways. The book is the great case study in the corruption of high-modernist power.

recommendations.item: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
recommendations.creator: Jane Jacobs
recommendations.context: Jacobs' classic on what makes cities actually live.
recommendations.reason: The opposite philosophy to Robert Moses — an organic appreciation for spontaneous order and metis. Scott himself draws intensively on Jacobs in Seeing Like a State. A great writer; everyone should read her.

recommendations.creator: Alain Bertaud
recommendations.context: Bertaud's book applying economic thinking to urban planning.
recommendations.reason: What happens when solid economic thinking is brought to cities. Exposes the follies of high modernism and respects metis — the way streets actually function, the way trees actually grow. Coolest fact: Bertaud isn't an economist by training; he's one of the renaissance men whose mind spans domains, like Scott himself.

recommendations.creator: Peter Wohlleben
recommendations.context: A book about how trees communicate and live with each other in mature forests.
recommendations.reason: Triggered by Ajay's account of Prussian scientific forestry. Wohlleben shows that you cannot just plant 40 trees together and call it an ecosystem — natural forests stand for hundreds of years with all the roots talking to each other, communicating, defending each other. Tackles the deeper hubris that humans are super-cool when in fact the natural world is so advanced in ways we cannot fathom.

recommendations.creator: Girish Karnad
recommendations.context: Karnad's 1960s play about Muhammad bin Tughlaq's high-modernist follies — shifting capitals, changing currencies — written as veiled commentary on Nehruvian socialism.
recommendations.reason: A play that lets you read Indian high-modernism backwards through the figure of a 14th-century sultan. Tughlaq's failures — the shift to Daulatabad, the token currency — are the original Indian template of the grand scheme; in the mid-60s, Karnad's Indian audience could feel the resonance with their own time.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the Deng Xiaoping motto used in this episode — 'cross the river by feeling the stones.' Scott-aligned in spirit: make small moves, do things you can undo, bring humility to coercive state power.

recommendations.creator: The Velvet Underground (Lou Reed and band)
recommendations.context: The cultural metaphor that opens the episode — the band of which it was said that only thirty people bought their albums and all thirty became musicians.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's frame for thinking about James C Scott — the Velvet Underground of ideas. A profound dominant influence on the people who go on to be dominant influences on the world, even if his name draws a 'James who? Scott who?' from the general public. The biggest compliment Ajay can give Lou Reed is to say the Velvet Underground are the James C Scott of music.

core_ideas.explanation: Seeing, for a state, is not the instinctive mammalian seeing of one human looking at another. It is a bureaucratic mapping from a state of nature into a written entry in a document, on which policy then acts. This is genuinely hard: people don't want to be seen (because the state may use the information against them in taxation, conscription, surveillance), and bureaucracies have their own incentive failures (discretion, principal-agent, shakedowns, opacity). Legibility is therefore a costly and political act, not a free technical one.
core_ideas.quote: Seeing by a bureaucracy is a mapping from a state of nature to a state action.

core_ideas.concept: State Legibility Schemes Have Unintended Consequences
core_ideas.explanation: When a state, sick of dealing with the messy richness of the real world, coerces a territory into being more legible to it — registering land, issuing unique IDs, demanding new forms of data — bad things tend to follow. Sometimes the state then abuses the visibility it has created. Sometimes the very flattening required to make life legible (one owner per plot of land, one cropping pattern, one road grid) destroys the Burkean web of overlapping rights and arrangements that made life work. The lesson is not that states should never see — it is that legibility is a complex and difficult journey that should never be granted carte blanche.
core_ideas.quote: State legibility schemes have unintended consequences.

core_ideas.concept: Reverse Legibility — The State Should Be Legible to Us
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's contribution: legibility flows the wrong way. The default has been to ask how visible we should be to the state. The right question is how visible the state should be to us. The state exists to serve us, not to rule us; the natural direction of legibility is government becoming utterly transparent and accountable to citizens. Normalising state surveillance of citizens is a 'deep perversion of the course of things.'
core_ideas.quote: We don't need to be legible to them. The state needs to be legible to us.

core_ideas.explanation: The natural extension of reverse-legibility: every act of non-deletion of data by the state should require explicit authorisation by the people, exactly as every act of state coercion already does. The baseline should be that data acquired by the state (tolls, payments, location pings) is deleted within seconds; any retention is the exception, and the state must stand on bended knee to extend it. This is the missing constitutional principle for the data age.
core_ideas.quote: Just as we say for every act of state coercion it's got to be authorised by the people, in similar fashion every act of non-deletion of data should be authorised by the people.

core_ideas.explanation: Modernism is good — secular, individualistic, an environment of freedom, individuals engaging individuals as full persons. High modernism is something completely different. It is the belief that scientists and engineers have a superior claim upon knowledge of society, that they should therefore reshape society through centrally controlled top-down schemes backed by the coercive power of an authoritarian state. It is one India 1X. It carries the borrowed prestige of science, but the science is mostly false confidence — and people respond to incentives by smirking and quietly undermining the scheme.
core_ideas.quote: It's like popularity and populism — almost opposite things.

core_ideas.explanation: James C Scott's English borrowing of a Greek word. Metis is deep, experiential, tacit knowledge that is not transferable in a book. It is intensely local — move a few hundred kilometres and the knowledge changes. It is the wisdom of the ecologist, the cyclist near the sprint finish, the village land-user; it cannot be tossed from above as a manual. Most knowledge about human society is metis. The opposite of high modernism is humility before metis.
core_ideas.quote: It is not knowledge in a book. You have to be there, you have to do things.

core_ideas.explanation: Scott's framework for when grand schemes destroy lives at scale: (1) a high-modernist philosophy that believes in top-down imposition; (2) the use of state power to render the world legible; (3) an authoritarian state; (4) a civil society that is prostrate and unable to push back. When all four come together, you get the worst outcomes. As development advice: in a country with an authoritarian government and weak civil society, be especially cautious about aiding, abetting, or encouraging high-modernist tendencies and state-legibility expansion.
core_ideas.quote: Watch out for these four things.

core_ideas.concept: Prussian Scientific Forestry — The Canonical Example
core_ideas.explanation: The canonical Scott parable, equally British-colonial in India. The forest is reduced to one purpose: cubic metres of timber. Plant a monoculture in clean rows; run hundred-year experiments to find optimal spacing; call it scientific. But the word 'science' is being abused — this is in fact ignorance of ecology. A natural forest is a resilient web of fungi, micronutrients, insects, ephemerals, shrubs, and trees in symbiosis; a tree-farm collapses on the fifth rotation as the soil is exhausted and a single fungus or insect can wipe it out. You imposed legibility — you can count the 1,000 trees — but you destroyed the forest. Explaining a joke is dissecting a frog.
core_ideas.quote: When people in the world of policy use the word science, you should start getting suspicious.

core_ideas.concept: Mao's Sparrows and Other Famous Failures
core_ideas.explanation: High modernism produces a recurring iconography of disaster. Mao's Four Pests campaign decreed all sparrows be killed for eating crops; sparrows ate locusts, locusts proliferated, crops were destroyed, millions starved. Stalin's collectivisation killed Ukrainian farmers and locked the USSR into commodity fragility for decades. Brasília was a city designed top-down that does not function as a city. India's Green Revolution succeeded narrowly on grain output and failed broadly: pesticide-poisoned groundwater, cancer belts in Punjab and Haryana, a groundwater crisis, farmers struggling to make a living, and a national diet over-stuffed with starch.
core_ideas.quote: It's an example of a grand scheme and it fits all the pieces and it fits the theory.

core_ideas.explanation: The standard Indian story celebrates the Green Revolution as a triumph that ended PL-480 dependence. The Scott-lens reading is harsher. MSP, fertiliser subsidy, free electricity for pumps, particular cultivars of rice and wheat — a high-modernist bundle imposed top-down. On longer horizons it has worked badly. Punjab and Haryana have pesticide-poisoned groundwater and cancer belts. Farmers there are not doing well; the Netherlands is the area of Haryana and exports 140 billion dollars of food. And we filled the Indian belly with starch when modern health policy would have prized protein, micronutrients, vegetables, fruit. An organic food system would have evolved differently.
core_ideas.quote: We filled up the bellies of the people of India with starch.

core_ideas.concept: Bandra Kurla and the Failure of Planned Financial Centres
core_ideas.explanation: Bandra Kurla Complex in Bombay was designed top-down as a financial centre. It became a bunch of corporate towers without coffee shops or pavements where shops can flourish. That isn't a financial centre. A financial centre is people having conversations over coffee. The lesson generalises: in urban planning, the right answer is roughly Bimal Patel's — about 40% of the land for streets and parks, the rest left to the people to decide. No master plan. On private land, owners do what they want. Top-down setbacks, parking rules, designated land-uses — central planning in a coat — produce dead urban forms.
core_ideas.quote: A financial centre is people. It is conversations over coffee.

core_ideas.explanation: There is no one-size-fits-all answer to whether a state-legibility mechanism is safe. It depends on where the country sits on something like the Freedom House ranking. Electronic payments are reasonably safe in Norway because rule of law and checks-and-balances make the data hard to weaponise; in North Korea they are a prison because every payment is surveilled. The research programme of the next hundred years is to build the table — what mechanism is appropriate at rank 1-10, at 30-40, at 100+. Note also that biometric ID systems tend to appear in relatively authoritarian developing countries, not advanced democracies — that itself is a clue.
core_ideas.quote: Certain systems should not be in certain countries.

core_ideas.explanation: India is 3.3 million square kilometres, a thousand locales. By definition, one dictator instructing all of India is a recipe for trouble. The Constitution of India is too centralising. The principle of subsidiarity — every function of government should be performed at the lowest level at which it can possibly be done — is the correct response to high modernism at country scale. A monetary union and one military make sense; almost everything else should be local. Mass transport in Bombay is Bombay expertise; mass transport in Pune is Pune expertise. The arrogance of having built the Delhi Metro does not entitle you to dictate metro design to every Indian city.
core_ideas.quote: Push subsidiarity. Every function of government should be done at the lowest level of government at which it can possibly be done.

core_ideas.concept: The European Union as the Lab of Decentralised Globalisation
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's counterintuitive admiration: the EU is the lab of globalisation done right. People, goods, services, and capital all move freely. But on substantive policy the EU is radically decentralised — abortion legal in one country, illegal in another; each member state writes its own laws. If you don't like Portugal, go live in France. There is no single government of Europe trying to micromanage the continent. The free-movement-plus-decentralisation combination is the inversion of the high-modernist instinct that with integration must come uniformity.
core_ideas.quote: It's not a single government of Europe that will micromanage the entire continent.

core_ideas.concept: Why the Late 1990s Needed This Book
core_ideas.explanation: Seeing Like a State landed in 1998, after the Berlin Wall (1989), after the USSR's collapse (1991), inside the early internet revolution. Many in successful democracies felt the great ideological battles were over and treated the moment as an opening for technocratic refashioning of state and society — a quiet drift back toward social engineering. People had lost their connections to the foundations of 20th-century freedom (Friedman, Hayek). And in places where scientists and engineers are treated with disproportionate respect, this drift was strongest. Scott's book was a corrective: yes, you have won the cold war; no, the answer is not to become a little bit more like the USSR.
core_ideas.quote: It almost felt like, now that the USSR is gone, let's be a little bit more like the USSR.

core_ideas.concept: Seeing Like a State as an Engine for Thinking
core_ideas.explanation: The deepest claim of the episode: Scott's vocabulary — state legibility, high modernism, metis, the four-part test — is not a theory of one thing. It is an engine you carry into other domains. Apply it to firms (imperial vs. adaptive), to forestry, to urban policy, to cycling, to ID systems, to development advice in authoritarian regimes, even to YouTube content strategy. Once the toolkit is in your brain, the world becomes more legible — to you.
core_ideas.quote: It's an engine for thinking about the world.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's twist on the famous Newton line: 'We all stand on the shoulders of giants. The other quote — and the reason I'm laughing — is that I couldn't get anywhere because giants were standing on my shoulders.'

Amit on what the proposed EIE T-shirt would have to be: 'You can only buy the t-shirt if you're at the triple XL — because how will the words fit?' (the slogan being 'State legibility schemes have unintended consequences').
Amit's mishearing of the term: 'When I first heard the phrase high modernism, I thought it basically means that you wear shirt-pant and you do drugs.'
Ajay on the rhetoric of 'science' in policy: 'Whenever anybody says scientific, I am like, dude, don't pull the science card.'
Amit on the only acceptable 'one India, 1X' scheme: 'One India, one YouTube show is an idea I can get behind.'

On translation parity: Amit notes EIE is available in ten languages, but Susan's request to send a Malayalam version revealed YouTube was supporting Hindi but not Malayalam. 'If you keep going like this, you will have serious south Indian secessionist problems.'
Amit asking Ajay to explain his open-mindedness: 'You're a nice guy — how can you be a great thinker?' Ajay: 'Niceness and great-thinking are orthogonal. I didn't mean they're negatively correlated.'
Ajay's escalation game on recommendations: 'In the next episode, I will give you nine recommendations.' Amit: 'Satyanash.'

'The Velvet Underground of ideas' — only thirty people bought their albums and all thirty became musicians. Ajay's metaphor for James C Scott: read by few, dominant influence on the people who themselves dominantly influence the world.
'The Velvet Revolution was named after them' — the 1989 Czechoslovak transition reportedly took its name from the band, knitting Vaclav Havel's politics to Lou Reed's sound.
'In computer science we stand on each other's shoulders' — a Unix fortune cited by Ajay as a kinder version of the Newtonian line.

'Cross the river by feeling the stones' — Deng Xiaoping's reform motto, used as a chapter title in Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic. The opposite of high-modernism: small moves, things you can undo.
'Explaining a joke is like dissecting a frog — you can understand it, but it kills the frog.' Used by Ajay to describe Prussian scientific forestry: you imposed legibility, but you killed the forest.

PC Mahalanobis and the Mahalanobis distance — Ajay's example of someone with phenomenal raw intellectual firepower whose social-engineering ideas were 'phenomenally wrong.' The paradox of the smart high-modernist.
Tughlaq's shift of the capital to Daulatabad — invoked as the 14th-century template of high modernism in India, and the subject of Girish Karnad's 1960s play that doubled as commentary on Nehru.
The Holodomor framed as a state-legibility scheme — Stalin's 1932 collectivisation as the seed of the 1991 Ukrainian referendum where 90% voted to leave Russia.
Brasília as the canonical failed planned city — 'some bloke in Delhi who thought why don't we go to Daulatabad and shift the capital,' but for South America.
'Bandra Kurla Complex doesn't have room for coffee shops' — Ajay's stinging critique of Bombay's planned financial centre.
'Le Corbusier himself made it' — Amit's birth in Chandigarh as a personal cameo from one of the villains of high modernism.
